lessons.title: Hard conversations: anger, bad news, and the parent
lessons.body:
## Three conversations that go wrong the same way

The angry husband, the family who has just been told someone died, and the parent of a sick child all fail for one reason: the provider talks too much, too fast, and too early. In every one of them the fix is the same shape, so learn the shape once.

## The angry family member

Anger at a scene is almost never about you. It is about helplessness, guilt for not calling sooner, or a previous bad experience with the health system.

The sequence that works is **listen, name, apologize for the experience, then act**.

- Listen without defending for at least `30` seconds, even if the content is unfair. Interrupting to correct a fact resets the clock.
- Name it: "You are furious that it took eleven minutes for us to get here."
- Apologize for the experience without admitting fault: "I'm sorry that wait felt endless. I would be angry too." That is not a legal admission; it is an acknowledgment.
- Then give them a job and a fact. "I need her medication list. We are leaving for the hospital in four minutes."

Never say "calm down," never say "you need to," and never debate response times on scene. If the anger is aimed at another agency or a prior provider, do not join in and do not defend. Say "I can't speak to what happened before I got here" and move.

## Breaking bad news, at the EMT level

You will not be delivering diagnoses, but you will be the person in the room when the resuscitation stops or when family asks the question directly. Use plain, unambiguous words, then stop talking.

1. **Prepare.** Move to a private space if one exists, sit down, and bring the right person, ideally the physician or crew chief with you.
2. **Warning shot.** "I have some very difficult news." One sentence of warning lets the brain get ready.
3. **The news, in plain words.** "He died." Not "passed," not "we lost him," not "he didn't make it." Softened words get misheard as hope.
4. **Silence.** Count to ten in your head. Do not fill it. This is the hardest skill in this lesson.
5. **Respond to the emotion, not the facts.** "This is a shock." "Take whatever time you need."
6. **Concrete next step.** What happens now, who will come, whether they can see the body, who to call.

Do not say "I know how you feel," "he's in a better place," "at least it was quick," or "everything happens for a reason." Each one puts your comfort ahead of theirs.

> **Trap:** Do not answer "did he suffer?" or "could we have done something?" with speculation. "He was not awake for any of it, and the doctor can tell you more" is honest. Guessing creates guilt that lasts decades.

## The parent of a sick child

A frightened parent is a source of data and the key to the exam. Treat them as a partner and say so early: "You know her better than anyone. What is different about her right now?"

Tell the parent what you are doing before each step, keep the child on their lap when the child is stable, and never contradict a parent in front of the child. If a parent is so panicked that they are frightening the child, give them a task away from the child's face.

Take "she isn't acting right" seriously as a clinical finding. A parent's alarm about a child who looks unremarkable to you is one of the more reliable signs in pediatrics.

> **Key:** In all three conversations: fewer words, plain words, then silence. Silence is not empty; it is where the other person catches up.
keyPoints: Angry family: listen 30 seconds, name the emotion, apologize for the experience, then give a job and a fact.
Apologizing for an experience is not an admission of fault, and it de-escalates faster than any explanation.
Bad news: warning shot, plain words like died, then silence for ten seconds.
Never say 'I know how you feel', 'at least it was quick', or anything that speculates about suffering.
A parent's statement that the child is not acting right is a clinical finding, not anxiety.

checks.q: A husband is shouting that your response took too long. What is the best first move?
choices: Explain the dispatch timeline in detail
Listen without defending, then name the emotion and apologize for the experience
Tell him you need him to calm down so you can work
Ask him to wait outside
checks.why: Defending facts early escalates. Listening, naming, and acknowledging the experience converts an obstacle into someone who will hand you the medication list.

checks.q: Which phrasing is correct when telling a family a patient has died?
choices: We did everything we could and he passed on
He didn't make it, I'm sorry
He died. I am so sorry.
He is no longer with us
checks.why: Softened language gets misheard as hope in a shocked brain. The plain word, followed by silence, is the kindest version.

checks.q: A mother says her 3-year-old is 'just not acting right' but the child looks well to you. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Parental anxiety to be reassured away
A clinical finding that warrants careful assessment and transport discussion
A reason to shorten the exam
An indication the parent should not ride along
checks.why: Parents detect subtle changes before providers do, and children compensate until they crash. Treat the statement as data.

lessons.title: Refusals that are not simple
lessons.body:
## The easy refusal is not the one that hurts you

A sober, oriented adult with normal vitals who declines transport is documented and released. The refusals that end in lawsuits and deaths are the three below, and all three turn on one question: does this person have capacity for **this specific decision, right now**?

## The intoxicated patient

Alcohol and drugs do not automatically remove capacity, and they do not automatically preserve it. There is no blood alcohol number that decides it, and breath testing is not the standard.

What decides it is function. Can the patient state what happened, what you are worried about, what could happen if they stay, and why they are choosing that? Ask them to say it back in their own words. "If I walk away tonight, I could have a bleed in my head and die in my sleep, and I'm accepting that" demonstrates capacity. "Yeah yeah, I'm fine, leave me alone" does not.

Also weigh the risk. The higher the stakes, the higher the bar for capacity. A refusal of an ice pack is not a refusal of transport after a head strike on a blood thinner.

If they lack capacity and are at real risk, treat under **implied consent**, involve police if needed for safety, and contact online medical direction. Document the specific words and behavior that led you to conclude capacity was absent.

> **Trap:** "He signed the form" protects nobody if the chart shows a patient who could not repeat the risks back. A signature from someone without capacity is worth less than no signature at all.

## The patient with dementia

Dementia is a spectrum, not a switch. A patient with mild dementia may retain capacity for simple decisions. What you are looking for is the same four abilities: understand, appreciate, reason, communicate a consistent choice.

Check against baseline with a caregiver, and look for a legally authorized decision maker. In New Jersey that may be a health care representative named in a **proxy directive**, a court-appointed guardian, or the person named on a **POLST**. A patient who cannot decide is not automatically refusing; you need whoever holds the authority. If nobody is available and there is an emergency, implied consent applies.

Repeating the question a few minutes later is a legitimate test. A consistent choice is one of the four capacity elements, and a patient whose answer changes every two minutes is not making a decision.

## The minor

In New Jersey a person under `18` cannot consent or refuse for themselves except in defined situations. A parent or legal guardian decides.

**Emancipated minors** decide for themselves: married, pregnant or already a parent, on active military duty, or emancipated by a court. New Jersey also allows minors to consent independently for certain categories such as treatment for sexually transmitted infections and substance use treatment.

Problems you will actually meet:

- **A hurt child with a babysitter or coach.** That adult is usually not a legal guardian and cannot refuse for the child. Reach the parent by phone, document the call, and treat under implied consent if you cannot.
- **A parent refusing care for a child you believe is seriously ill.** Contact medical direction immediately, and involve police. Refusal that endangers a child can become a child protective services report; New Jersey requires any person with reasonable cause to report suspected neglect to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE.
- **A 17-year-old alone who says they are fine.** They cannot refuse. Reach a guardian.

## The universal protections

Assess fully, document capacity with evidence, name the specific risks including death where real, offer alternatives, involve online medical direction for anything high risk, get a signature and an independent witness, and write the whole conversation with quotes. Then, if they still refuse, tell them plainly: "Call 911 again for any reason, including changing your mind. We will come back."

> **On the exam:** Any refusal vignette that includes hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, or significant intoxication is testing whether you recognize that capacity is absent.
keyPoints: No alcohol level decides capacity; function does, tested by having the patient repeat the risks in their own words.
The higher the risk of the decision, the higher the capacity bar.
Dementia is a spectrum; check baseline with a caregiver and find the legally authorized decision maker.
Minors under 18 cannot refuse unless emancipated; babysitters and coaches are not guardians.
A parent endangering a child by refusing triggers medical direction, police, and a 1-877-NJ-ABUSE report.

checks.q: A 40-year-old with slurred speech after three beers struck his head and says only 'I'm fine, go away.' What is the correct read?
choices: He has capacity because he is awake and speaking
He lacks demonstrated capacity because he cannot state the risks he is accepting
Capacity is determined by breath alcohol level
A signed refusal form resolves the issue
checks.why: Capacity is functional. Without evidence he understands and accepts the specific risk of an intracranial bleed, the refusal is not valid, and a signature does not cure it.

checks.q: A 15-year-old soccer player is injured at practice; only the coach is present. Who can refuse transport?
choices: The coach, as the responsible adult present
The 15-year-old, since he is a teenager
Nobody present; reach a parent or guardian and treat under implied consent if unreachable
The athletic trainer
checks.why: A coach is not a legal guardian and a non-emancipated minor cannot refuse. Contact the guardian, document the attempt, and act under implied consent for an emergency.

checks.q: An 82-year-old with moderate dementia gives a different answer about transport every few minutes. What does this demonstrate?
choices: A firm refusal that must be honored
Failure to communicate a consistent choice, so capacity is absent for this decision
Full capacity, because she is verbal
That she must be restrained
checks.why: Communicating a consistent choice is one of the four capacity elements. Seek the authorized decision maker or act under implied consent for an emergency.

lessons.title: Two charts, same call
lessons.body:
## The same twenty minutes, written twice

The call: `1412` dispatch, `62`-year-old man, chest pressure. Below is what a weak narrative looks like, then a strong one for the identical call, then the rules extracted from the difference.

## Narrative A: the one that will not hold up

"Responded to a chest pain call. Pt was a 62 yo M c/o chest pain. He looked bad and was really anxious. Wife said he has heart problems. Gave O2 and aspirin. Pt refused to calm down. Vitals were stable. Transported priority to the hospital without incident. Care transferred to ED staff."

Everything wrong with it: no times, no numbers, no chief complaint in his words, no OPQRST, no allergies, "looked bad" and "stable" are opinions with no content, no aspirin dose, no response to treatment, "refused to calm down" is a judgment, and "ED staff" names nobody.

## Narrative B: the one that does

"Dispatched `1412`, on scene `1418`, patient contact `1420`. Found `62`-year-old male seated upright in a kitchen chair, pale and diaphoretic. Chief complaint in his words: 'It feels like someone is standing on my chest.'

OPQRST: onset `1330` while carrying groceries, gradual, constant since. Worse with walking, not changed by position or palpation. Described as pressure. Radiates to left jaw. Severity `8/10` on arrival. Denies shortness of breath at rest, denies nausea, denies syncope.

SAMPLE: allergies none known. Medications atorvastatin, metoprolol, lisinopril. History of myocardial infarction 2019 with two stents, hypertension, hyperlipidemia. Last oral intake coffee `0800`. Events: symptoms began during exertion.

Exam: skin pale, cool, diaphoretic. Lungs clear bilaterally at four points. No jugular venous distension. Radial pulses equal bilaterally. No peripheral edema.

Vitals `1422`: HR `96` regular, BP `148/88`, RR `20`, SpO2 `94%` room air. Vitals `1435`: HR `88`, BP `138/84`, RR `18`, SpO2 `97%` on `2 L` nasal cannula.

Treatment: oxygen `2 L` nasal cannula at `1423` for saturation `94%`, saturation rose to `97%`. Aspirin `324 mg` chewed at `1424`, no adverse effect. Patient assisted with own nitroglycerin `0.4 mg` sublingual at `1426` per protocol with BP `148/88` documented before administration; pain decreased from `8/10` to `5/10` at `1432`. Position of comfort, semi-Fowler.

ALS intercept requested `1421`, met at `1433`. Transport began `1430`. Arrived `1441`. Care transferred at `1443` to RN K. Alvarez, bed 4, verbal report given including vitals trend and nitroglycerin response."

## What separates them

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| "Looked bad" | pale, cool, diaphoretic |
| "Vitals stable" | two timed sets with actual numbers |
| "Gave aspirin" | `324 mg` chewed at `1424`, no adverse effect |
| "Chest pain" | the patient's own quoted words |
| "Refused to calm down" | quoted statement, or nothing at all |
| "Transferred to ED staff" | name, role, bed, and time |

> **Key:** Every claim in a narrative should be either a number, a quote, or an observation another person could have seen. Adjectives are where charts fail.

> **Trap:** "Without incident" and "tolerated well" say nothing and are read as "I did not reassess." Replace them with the reassessment numbers.

> **On shift:** Write the narrative before you clear, while the times are still in your head. Reconstructed times are the first thing an attorney attacks.
keyPoints: Every narrative claim should be a number, a direct quote, or an observation a second person could verify.
Vitals belong in the chart as at least two timed sets so the trend is visible.
Every medication needs dose, route, time, and the patient's response.
Transfer of care is documented by name, role, location, and time, never as 'ED staff'.
Phrases like stable, looked bad, tolerated well, and without incident carry no information.

checks.q: Which entry best replaces 'patient looked bad'?
choices: Patient appeared unwell and anxious
Patient in obvious distress
Skin pale, cool, and diaphoretic; speaks in short phrases
Patient was sick-looking on arrival
checks.why: It gives observations another provider could have seen and verified. The others are the same opinion reworded.

checks.q: What is missing from 'Gave aspirin, patient tolerated well'?
choices: Nothing, this is adequate
Dose, route, time, and the documented response
The brand name
The prescribing physician
checks.why: Medication entries require dose, route, time, and effect. 'Tolerated well' is not a documented response.

checks.q: Why is 'care transferred to ED staff' inadequate?
choices: It is too long
It names no person or role, so there is no proof care was accepted by an equal or higher level
It should be in the vitals section
It requires a patient signature
checks.why: Transfer of care must be to a named person at an equal or higher level. Without a name, role, and time, the record cannot rebut an abandonment claim.

lessons.title: A radio phrase library for five call types
lessons.body:
## Say it the same way every time

The reason radio reports collapse under stress is that people compose them live. Learn a template per call type, fill in blanks, and the report survives adrenaline. Each one below runs about `25` to `35` seconds.

Mechanics first: key the microphone, wait one full second, then speak, or the first word is cut. Hold the microphone `2` to `3` inches from your mouth, speak slightly slower than normal, no names, no opinions, no humor, and nothing you would not want played back in court.

## Medical

"Medic 4 to County, en route to you with a `68`-year-old female, ETA `10` minutes. Chief complaint is shortness of breath for `2` days, worse tonight. She is alert and oriented, tripoding, speaking in three-word sentences. Vitals: heart rate `118`, blood pressure `164/92`, respirations `28`, saturation `88%` on room air, now `94%` on CPAP. History of COPD and heart failure, on home oxygen at `2` liters. We have given one albuterol treatment with partial improvement. Requesting a respiratory-ready room."

## Trauma, in MIST form

"Rescue 2 to Trauma, ETA `7` minutes, `24`-year-old male, trauma alert. Mechanism: unrestrained driver, frontal impact at highway speed, prolonged extrication, `12` inches of intrusion. Injuries: obvious left femur deformity, seat belt sign absent, decreased breath sounds on the right, abrasions to face. Signs: heart rate `132`, blood pressure `88/50`, respirations `26`, saturation `90%`, GCS `13`. Treatment: high-flow oxygen, tourniquet to the left thigh at `2142`, pelvic binder, spinal precautions, warmed. Requesting the trauma team on arrival."

## Cardiac arrest

"Medic 1 to County, working cardiac arrest, `57`-year-old male, ETA `6` minutes. Witnessed arrest, bystander CPR started immediately, down time approximately `14` minutes. Initial rhythm ventricular fibrillation, three shocks delivered, currently in pulseless electrical activity. CPR in progress with a mechanical device, king airway placed with waveform capnography reading `18`. IV access established, epinephrine times three. No return of spontaneous circulation at this time. Requesting the resuscitation bay."

## Pediatric

"Unit 6 to Children's, ETA `12` minutes with a `3`-year-old female, weight approximately `15` kilograms. Chief complaint is fever and difficulty breathing for `1` day. Pediatric assessment triangle: appearance sleepy but consolable, increased work of breathing with retractions and nasal flaring, skin mottled. Vitals: heart rate `168`, respirations `48`, saturation `91%` on room air now `97%` on blow-by oxygen, temperature `39.4` Celsius, capillary refill `3` seconds. Glucose `88`. Mother reports decreased wet diapers today. Requesting a pediatric room."

## Refusal notification

"Medic 3 to Medical Control, requesting a physician consult on a refusal. `61`-year-old male, fall from a `6`-foot ladder, struck his head, no loss of consciousness reported. He is alert and oriented times four, vitals heart rate `78`, blood pressure `142/86`, respirations `16`, saturation `98%`, glucose `104`. He takes apixaban. He has repeated back the risk of intracranial bleeding and states he understands he could die. He is declining transport. Requesting your guidance and your name for documentation."

> **Key:** Every report answers the same three questions in order: who and how sick, what you found, what you need from the receiving facility.

> **Trap:** Do not narrate the story chronologically on the radio. "We arrived and the daughter said..." wastes the window. The narrative belongs in the chart.

> **On the exam:** Radio-report questions usually test what does not belong: names, opinions, unconfirmed diagnoses, and social history are all wrong answers.
keyPoints: Use a fixed template per call type so the report survives adrenaline; each runs 25 to 35 seconds.
Key the microphone, wait one second, then speak, 2 to 3 inches away and slightly slow.
Trauma uses MIST and leads with mechanism; cardiac arrest leads with down time, rhythm, and interventions.
Pediatric reports include weight in kilograms and the pediatric assessment triangle.
Every report ends with what you need: trauma team, cath lab, respiratory room, or a physician consult.

checks.q: Which element belongs in a trauma radio report but not usually in a medical one?
choices: Vital signs
Mechanism of injury, in detail
Estimated time of arrival
Treatment given
checks.why: Mechanism predicts injuries the receiving team has not yet seen, which is why MIST leads with it. The other three appear in every report.

checks.q: Which item should never be transmitted over the radio?
choices: The patient's oxygen saturation
The estimated time of arrival
The patient's name and address
The treatment already given
checks.why: Identifiers are not needed for the receiving team to prepare and radio traffic is not private. Clinical data and logistics are appropriate.

checks.q: A cardiac arrest report should lead with which information?
choices: The patient's past medical history
The family's wishes
Whether the arrest was witnessed, the down time, the initial rhythm, and current status
The medication list
checks.why: Witnessed status, down time, and initial rhythm drive the receiving team's expectations and preparation more than any other data.

lessons.title: HIPAA on the street: twelve verdicts
lessons.body:
## The rule is simple, the situations are not

Protected health information may be shared for treatment, payment, and operations, limited to the **minimum necessary**. Everything below is an application of that one sentence. Read the situation, decide, then read the verdict.

## The twelve

1. **You tell the receiving nurse the patient's HIV status because it is on the medication list.** Permitted. Treatment purpose, and it is relevant to the receiving clinician's care.
2. **You tell the fire crew that helped lift the patient what her diagnosis turned out to be.** Not permitted. They are no longer involved in care, and curiosity is not a treatment purpose.
3. **A police officer at a motor vehicle crash asks whether the driver had been drinking.** Not permitted on your own. Share scene and safety information; clinical findings generally need patient authorization, a legal mandate such as a gunshot wound report, or a warrant or court order. Refer the request up.
4. **You call your supervisor to discuss whether a call should be reviewed for quality.** Permitted. Health care operations.
5. **You look up the chart of a coworker who was brought in last night, because you are worried about him.** Not permitted. Access without a treatment relationship is a breach, the audit log records it, and concern is not an exception.
6. **You post a photo of a wrecked car with no patient visible and the caption "rough one tonight."** High risk and generally treated as a violation. If the crash is identifiable locally, the patient is identifiable, and most agencies prohibit scene photography outright.
7. **You discuss a case in the ambulance bay while a family from another patient walks past.** Not permitted. Incidental disclosure becomes a violation when reasonable safeguards are not used. Move inside and lower your voice.
8. **A patient's adult daughter, who is the named health care representative, asks about her mother's condition.** Permitted to the extent of her authority, after you verify identity and the role.
9. **A caller says he is the patient's brother and asks what hospital you took him to.** Not without verification. Identity verification is required, and facility directory rules govern what a hospital may confirm. Do not disclose by phone from the field.
10. **You leave a completed PCR face-up on the counter at the nurses' station.** Not permitted. Unsecured PHI is a breach even if nobody reads it.
11. **You use a de-identified version of a case to teach a class, with no name, no date, and no location.** Permitted. Education is an operations purpose and de-identified information is not PHI.
12. **A reporter asks you at the scene what happened to the patient.** Not permitted. Refer to the public information officer. "I can't discuss patients" is the entire answer.

## The safeguards that prevent most of it

Lower your voice, close the curtain, turn the monitor, lock the screen, put the chart face-down, and never photograph a scene, a patient, or a monitor with a personal phone. The most common breaches are not malicious; they are volume and convenience.

> **Key:** Ask two questions: does this person need it to care for, bill for, or review this patient's care, and am I giving only the minimum needed? If either answer is no, stop.

> **Trap:** "I didn't say the name" does not protect you. If anyone in the community could identify the patient from the details, it is a disclosure.

> **On shift:** New hospital employees are audited. Looking up your own chart, a relative's chart, or a famous patient's chart is the single most common way technicians are fired in their first year.
keyPoints: Test every disclosure against treatment, payment, or operations, plus the minimum necessary standard.
Curiosity, concern, and having been on the call are not treatment purposes.
Police get scene and safety information; clinical details need authorization, a legal mandate, or a warrant.
De-identified teaching is permitted; identifiable scene photos and social posts are not.
Unsecured charts, hallway conversations, and self or family chart lookups are the most common real breaches.

checks.q: A firefighter who helped carry your patient later asks what the diagnosis was. What is the correct response?
choices: Share it, since he was on the call
Decline politely; he is no longer involved in the patient's care
Share it only if he promises confidentiality
Share it if the patient is not from your town
checks.why: Treatment purpose ends when involvement in care ends. Prior presence on a call does not create ongoing access.

checks.q: Which of these is a permitted disclosure?
choices: Telling your spouse about an unusual injury with identifying details
Posting a scene photo with no faces
Reporting the case in a quality improvement review with your supervisor
Confirming to a phone caller which hospital a patient went to
checks.why: Quality review is a health care operations purpose. The others are disclosures to people with no treatment, payment, or operations role, or without verified identity.

checks.q: You are worried about a coworker who was a patient last night. What may you do?
choices: Look at his chart since you know him
Ask a nurse to read you the chart
Ask him directly how he is, and never access the record
Look at only the vitals
checks.why: Any access without a treatment relationship is a breach, and audit logs capture it. Asking the person is the only permitted route.

lessons.title: Calling medical control and taking an order
lessons.body:
## Why the call exists

Your protocols are the physician medical director speaking to you in advance; those are **standing orders**, or offline medical direction. When a situation falls outside them, you reach a physician live. That is **online medical direction**, and the call has a structure because a physician who has never seen the patient must make a decision in under a minute.

Common reasons to call: a medication or intervention that requires physician authorization in your protocol, a high-risk refusal, an unusual destination decision, a request to withhold or terminate resuscitation, a patient whose presentation does not fit any protocol, and any time you want a second opinion and have the time to get one.

## How to make the call

1. **Decide what you want before you key up.** A request without an ask wastes both of your time.
2. **Identify.** Unit, your name and certification level, and that you are requesting online medical direction.
3. **Give a compressed report.** Age, complaint, two sets of vitals with times, pertinent history and medications, what you have already done and the response.
4. **State the request in one sentence.** "I am requesting permission to assist this patient with a second dose of his own nitroglycerin."
5. **Listen, then read back.** Repeat the order verbatim, including drug, dose, route, and any conditions. "Confirming: nitroglycerin `0.4 mg` sublingual, one dose, only if the systolic stays above `100`."
6. **Confirm you have it.** Wait for the physician to say yes, then act.
7. **Document.** The physician's name, the time of the order, the exact order, and the result. A verbal order you cannot attribute to a named physician is a problem later.

## If you disagree with the order

This happens, and there is a professional way through it.

State the concern with the observation first: "Doctor, I want to make sure you have this: his systolic is `84` and he is diaphoretic. Do you still want the nitroglycerin?" That gives the physician a chance to catch a missed detail, which is the usual explanation.

If the order is repeated and you still believe it is unsafe or outside your scope, say so plainly: "I am not comfortable with that order, and it is outside my scope as an EMT." You do not perform an order you believe is harmful or that exceeds your certification. Document the exchange factually, notify your supervisor, and follow your agency's process. You are never protected by "a doctor told me to" for something outside your legal scope.

## Orders you cannot take

No physician can expand your scope of practice over the radio. Scope is set by the state, in New Jersey by the Office of Emergency Medical Services. An order to perform a paramedic-level skill is not valid for an EMT no matter who gives it.

> **Key:** Report, one-sentence request, verbatim read-back, confirmation, then document the physician's name and the time.

> **Trap:** "Give him some oxygen and whatever else he needs" is not an order. Vague direction gets clarified before you act, not after.

> **On the exam:** The tested steps are read-back of the complete order and documentation of the ordering physician. Answers that have the EMT act first and confirm later are wrong.
keyPoints: Offline medical direction is your protocols; online is a live physician consult for what falls outside them.
Call structure: identify, compressed report, one-sentence request, verbatim read-back, confirmation, documentation.
Document the physician's name, the exact order, the time, and the result.
Voice a disagreement by leading with the observation, then decline plainly if the order is unsafe or out of scope.
No physician order can expand your state-defined scope of practice.

checks.q: A physician gives you a verbal order over the radio. What must you do before acting?
choices: Act immediately to save time
Repeat the order back verbatim and wait for confirmation
Write it down and act, confirming later
Ask your partner to verify it
checks.why: Verbatim read-back with confirmation closes the loop and catches misheard doses. Acting first and confirming later is how wrong-dose errors happen.

checks.q: An online physician orders a skill that is outside the EMT scope of practice in your state. What is correct?
choices: Perform it, since a physician authorized it
Decline, because a physician order cannot expand your legal scope
Perform it only if your partner agrees
Perform it and document that the physician ordered it
checks.why: Scope is set by the state, not by an individual physician. Performing an out-of-scope skill is a certification violation regardless of who ordered it.

checks.q: Which is the best way to question an order you believe is unsafe?
choices: Refuse without explanation
Restate the key observation and ask if the physician still wants the order
Perform it and report it afterward
Ask a different physician without saying why
checks.why: Leading with the observation usually reveals a detail the physician did not have, and it avoids framing the concern as an accusation.

lessons.title: Errors, near misses, and conflict on the crew
lessons.body:
## The system only learns about what gets reported

A **near miss** is an error that was caught before it reached the patient: the wrong medication drawn up and noticed, the wrong patient identified and corrected at the bedside. A **safety event** reached the patient, with or without harm. Both get reported, and the near miss is arguably more valuable, because you get the lesson without the injury.

Most organizations run some version of **just culture**, which separates three things:

- **Human error:** a slip by someone doing the right thing. The response is to fix the system, console the person, and move on.
- **At-risk behavior:** taking a shortcut whose risk you did not appreciate, such as skipping a second identifier because you were in a hurry. The response is coaching and removing the incentive to shortcut.
- **Reckless behavior:** conscious disregard of a known serious risk, such as working impaired. The response is discipline.

The practical consequence: reporting your own honest error almost never ends a career, and concealing one frequently does.

## What to do after an error

1. **Patient first.** Assess, treat, stabilize, tell the receiving clinician immediately and plainly.
2. **Tell your supervisor** before they hear it from someone else.
3. **Document facts in the chart:** what was given or done, the time, the patient's response, who was notified and when. Do not write "error" as a conclusion, do not speculate on cause, and never alter a prior entry.
4. **File the incident report** in the agency's separate system. It is not part of the medical record, so do not reference it in the chart.
5. **Participate in the review** honestly. Describe what you saw, not what you assume.

> **Trap:** Never correct a chart to make an error disappear. Amendments and audit trails are visible, and a concealed error is a far larger problem than the error itself.

## Conflict with a partner or a nurse

Disagreements happen in front of patients, which is where they do the most damage. Two rules: never argue clinical decisions in front of the patient, and never criticize another provider to a patient or family.

Use a simple script, sometimes taught as **DESC**, to raise an issue afterward:

- **Describe** the specific behavior: "On the last call, the stretcher straps were not secured before we moved."
- **Express** the concern using the effect, not a label: "I was worried about the patient sliding on the stairs."
- **Suggest** an alternative: "Can we do a straps check out loud before every move?"
- **Consequence,** stated positively: "That way neither of us has to think about it."

Do it privately, soon, once, and about the behavior rather than the person. If it is a patient safety issue in the moment, use the two-challenge rule instead: state the concern twice, and if it is not addressed, escalate up the chain immediately.

With a nurse who dismisses your handoff or your concern, the same structure works: observation, concern, specific request. "Her pressure dropped from `124` to `88` in ten minutes. I am concerned. Can you look at her now?" That is not insubordination, and refusing to escalate a deteriorating patient is not deference.

> **Key:** Report what nearly happened as readily as what did. The near miss is free information.

> **On shift:** Conflict handled in a hallway stays professional. Conflict handled at a bedside becomes part of the patient's experience, and sometimes part of a complaint.
keyPoints: A near miss is caught before reaching the patient and is still reported; it is the cheapest lesson available.
Just culture separates human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior, with different responses to each.
After an error: patient first, tell the receiving clinician, document facts, notify your supervisor, file the incident report separately.
Never conceal an error by altering a chart; audit trails make concealment worse than the error.
Use DESC privately for crew conflict, and the two-challenge rule with immediate escalation for safety issues.

checks.q: You realize you gave the correct medication to the wrong patient, who suffered no harm. What is the first action?
choices: File an incident report at the end of shift
Assess the patient and immediately tell the receiving clinician
Note it in the chart and move on
Discuss it with your partner first
checks.why: Patient safety comes before paperwork. The clinician taking over needs the information now to monitor for effects; reporting follows.

checks.q: Under just culture, what is the expected response to an honest human error?
choices: Discipline the individual
Fix the system and support the person
Remove the person from patient care permanently
No action at all
checks.why: Human error calls for system repair and consolation. Discipline is reserved for reckless behavior, such as conscious disregard of a known serious risk.

checks.q: Your partner disagrees with your treatment plan in front of the patient. What is the professional response?
choices: Argue the point until one of you concedes
Defer silently and complain later to a supervisor
Address the immediate safety issue if there is one, then discuss the disagreement privately using specific behavior
Ask the patient to decide
checks.why: Bedside arguments harm the patient's confidence and the chart. Safety issues are escalated in the moment; style disagreements are handled privately and specifically.

lessons.title: Health literacy, teach-back, and harder interpreter calls
lessons.body:
## Most patients do not understand what they were told

Roughly `9` in `10` adults in the United States have difficulty using health information that is written the way clinicians write it. That is not an intelligence problem; it is a vocabulary and stress problem. Add fear and it gets worse, which is exactly the condition every one of your patients is in.

The practical defaults:

- Aim for language a `5`th to `6`th grade reader would follow.
- Use short sentences with one idea each.
- Say the most important thing first and repeat it at the end.
- Use concrete nouns, not categories: "your water pill" beats "your diuretic," "the hospital across from the mall" beats the formal facility name.
- Replace numbers with comparisons where you can: "about the size of a quarter" instead of `2.5 cm`.

Avoid the words that reliably fail: "benign," "negative" (patients often hear bad), "positive" (patients often hear good), "acute," "NPO," "ambulate," "void," "hypertension" when you could say high blood pressure.

## Teach-back, done correctly

Teach-back is asking the patient to say the plan back in their own words. The wrong version, "Do you understand?", gets a yes from everybody, because saying no is embarrassing.

Put the burden on yourself: "I want to make sure I explained that well. Can you tell me what you are going to watch for tonight?" If the answer is wrong, re-explain differently and ask again. Two rounds is normal, and it is the only way to know a refusal conversation actually landed.

> **Key:** "Do you understand?" tests politeness. "Tell me what you will do" tests understanding.

## Signs someone cannot read what you handed them

People hide low literacy well. Watch for: "I forgot my glasses," handing the form to a relative, saying they will read it later, tracing a finger without reading, signing without looking, or filling forms incompletely. Never announce it. Offer to read it aloud to everyone as your routine: "I read these out loud for everybody, it is easier than the print."

## Interpreter calls that get complicated

Beyond the basics of using a qualified interpreter and never using a child, three situations cause trouble.

**The patient who speaks some English.** Partial fluency collapses under stress and pain. Use the interpreter for anything consequential: consent, refusal, risks, allergies, and the history. Offer the interpreter rather than asking whether they need one, since many patients decline out of embarrassment.

**Phone interpreting with an altered or hard-of-hearing patient.** Put the phone on speaker near the patient's better ear, keep segments to one sentence, and confirm with teach-back through the interpreter. Video interpretation is far better when available, and is required in practice for American Sign Language.

**The interpreter who starts summarizing.** You will hear a long patient response returned as three words. Say, "Please give me everything she said, word for word." Summarized interpretation loses the detail you are trying to collect.

Document the interpreter's name or identification number, the language, and the modality used. A refusal obtained through a family member who "speaks a little English" is a refusal you will not be able to defend.

> **On shift:** As a technician you will often be the person handing over discharge instructions. Read the first line out loud, then teach-back the one action that matters most: when to come back.
keyPoints: Write and speak at a 5th to 6th grade level, one idea per sentence, most important thing first and last.
Avoid benign, negative, positive, acute, NPO, ambulate, and void; use plain equivalents.
Teach-back means asking the patient to state the plan back, framed as checking your own explanation.
Low literacy is hidden by 'forgot my glasses' and signing without reading; read aloud as a routine for everyone.
Use an interpreter for anything consequential even with partial English fluency, and document name, language, and modality.

checks.q: Which question actually tests understanding?
choices: Do you understand what I told you?
Any questions?
I want to be sure I explained it well. What are you going to watch for tonight?
Does that make sense?
checks.why: Yes-or-no questions test politeness. Asking the patient to state the plan in their own words, with the burden framed on your explanation, tests comprehension.

checks.q: A patient with limited English says he does not need an interpreter for a refusal conversation. What should you do?
choices: Honor the preference and proceed in English
Use a bilingual family member instead
Offer and use a qualified interpreter, since consent and refusal require full comprehension
Write the risks down for him to read
checks.why: Partial fluency fails under stress, and an undefendable refusal is the result. Consequential conversations use a qualified interpreter regardless of preference.

checks.q: A patient says he forgot his glasses when handed a refusal form. What is the best response?
choices: Ask a family member to read it to him
Have him sign and explain later
Read it aloud as your routine practice for everyone and confirm with teach-back
Note that he declined to read it
checks.why: This is a common indicator of low literacy. Reading aloud for everyone avoids embarrassment and produces a documented, understood refusal.

cards.front: What is the four-step sequence for an angry family member?
cards.back: Listen without defending for 30 seconds, name the emotion, apologize for the experience without admitting fault, then give a concrete job and a fact.

cards.front: Is saying 'I'm sorry that wait felt endless' an admission of fault?
cards.back: No. Apologizing for an experience acknowledges the person's reality. Admitting fault is a statement that you or your agency did something wrong.

cards.front: What are the six steps for delivering bad news?
cards.back: Prepare and get private, give a warning shot, deliver the news in plain words, stay silent about ten seconds, respond to the emotion, give one concrete next step.

cards.front: Why say 'he died' instead of 'he passed' or 'he didn't make it'?
cards.back: A shocked brain hears softened language as ambiguity or hope. Plain words prevent a second, crueler round of confusion.

cards.front: Name four phrases never to say to a grieving family.
cards.back: 'I know how you feel,' 'he's in a better place,' 'at least it was quick,' and 'everything happens for a reason.' Each serves your comfort, not theirs.

cards.front: A family asks 'did he suffer?' What is the honest answer?
cards.back: Say only what you observed, such as that he was not awake, and refer the rest to the physician. Speculation creates guilt that lasts decades.

cards.front: How do you position a panicking parent who is frightening the child?
cards.back: Give them a specific task away from the child's face, such as gathering medications or meeting the crew at the door, without criticizing them in front of the child.

cards.front: Does a blood alcohol level determine capacity to refuse?
cards.back: No. Capacity is functional: can the patient state what happened, what you are worried about, what could happen, and why they choose otherwise. No number decides it.

cards.front: Why does a higher-risk decision require more evidence of capacity?
cards.back: The bar scales with the stakes. Declining an ice pack needs little; declining transport after a head strike on a blood thinner needs a demonstrated understanding of death risk.

cards.front: What is the value of a signed refusal from a patient without capacity?
cards.back: Essentially none, and it can be worse than nothing, because the chart then documents that you obtained a signature from someone who could not consent.

cards.front: How do you test for a 'consistent choice' in a patient with dementia?
cards.back: Ask again a few minutes later. An answer that changes every few minutes fails the communicate-a-consistent-choice element of capacity.

cards.front: Who can make decisions for an adult without capacity in New Jersey?
cards.back: A health care representative named in a proxy directive, a court-appointed guardian, or the representative named on a POLST. Otherwise, implied consent for the emergency.

cards.front: Can a babysitter, coach, or teacher refuse care for an injured child?
cards.back: No. They are not legal guardians. Contact the parent or guardian, document the attempt, and treat under implied consent if the child has an emergency.

cards.front: A parent refuses care for a child you believe is seriously ill. What do you do?
cards.back: Contact online medical direction immediately, involve police, and consider a report to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. Do not simply accept the refusal and leave.

cards.front: Why are 'stable' and 'tolerated well' useless in a narrative?
cards.back: They are conclusions with no content. They are read later as evidence you did not reassess. Replace them with timed numbers.

cards.front: What four pieces must accompany every medication in a PCR?
cards.back: Dose, route, time, and the patient's response, plus any value required before giving it, such as the blood pressure before nitroglycerin.

cards.front: How should transfer of care be documented?
cards.back: By name and role of the person accepting, the location, and the time: 'care transferred 1443 to RN K. Alvarez, bed 4, verbal report given.'

cards.front: What is the test for whether a narrative sentence is strong enough?
cards.back: It must be a number, a direct quote, or an observation another provider could have independently seen. Adjectives fail all three.

cards.front: Rewrite 'patient refused to calm down' properly.
cards.back: Quote it or drop it: 'Patient stated, I am not going anywhere with you.' The original is a judgment about the patient's character.

cards.front: How many sets of vitals should appear in a narrative and why?
cards.back: At least two, each timed, so the trend and the response to treatment are visible. One set proves nothing about direction.

cards.front: When should the narrative be written?
cards.back: Before you clear, while times are still accurate. Reconstructed times are the first thing challenged in a deposition.

cards.front: What are the radio mechanics that prevent a clipped first word?
cards.back: Key the microphone, wait one full second, then speak, holding it 2 to 3 inches away and slightly slower than normal speech.

cards.front: What three questions does every radio report answer, in order?
cards.back: Who and how sick, what you found, and what you need from the receiving facility.

cards.front: What leads a cardiac arrest radio report?
cards.back: Witnessed or unwitnessed, bystander CPR, estimated down time, initial rhythm, shocks delivered, current rhythm, airway and access, and whether circulation has returned.

cards.front: What two items are unique to a pediatric radio report?
cards.back: The child's weight in kilograms and the pediatric assessment triangle findings: appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin.

cards.front: What belongs in a refusal consult to medical control?
cards.back: Age, mechanism, full vitals including glucose, relevant medications such as anticoagulants, evidence of capacity in the patient's words, and a request for guidance plus the physician's name.

cards.front: Why is a chronological story the wrong shape for a radio report?
cards.back: The listener is deciding room, team, and speed. Leading with 'we arrived and the daughter said' spends the 30-second window before the decision data arrives.

cards.front: Name four things that never go over the radio.
cards.back: Patient names and addresses, opinions about the patient, unconfirmed diagnoses, and humor or profanity. Assume every transmission is recorded.

cards.front: Is telling the receiving nurse a patient's HIV status permitted?
cards.back: Yes, when relevant to continuing care. It is a treatment disclosure, limited by the minimum necessary standard.

cards.front: A fire crew that helped lift your patient asks the diagnosis later. Permitted?
cards.back: No. Their involvement in care has ended, and prior presence on a call does not create ongoing access. Curiosity is not a treatment purpose.

cards.front: May you look up a coworker's chart because you are worried about him?
cards.back: No. Access without a treatment relationship is a breach, audit logs capture it, and concern is not an exception. Ask the person directly.

cards.front: Is a scene photo without any patient visible safe to post?
cards.back: Generally no. If the incident is locally identifiable, the patient is identifiable. Most agencies prohibit scene photography outright.

cards.front: A caller claims to be the patient's brother and asks which hospital. What do you do?
cards.back: Do not disclose from the field. Identity cannot be verified by phone, and facility directory rules govern what a hospital may confirm.

cards.front: When is using a case to teach permitted?
cards.back: When it is de-identified: no name, no date, no location, nothing that lets anyone identify the patient. Education is an operations purpose.

cards.front: What is the two-question test before any disclosure?
cards.back: Does this person need it to treat, bill for, or review this patient's care, and am I giving only the minimum necessary? If either is no, stop.

cards.front: List the seven steps of an online medical direction call.
cards.back: Decide your ask, identify unit and level, give a compressed report, state the request in one sentence, read back verbatim, get confirmation, then document name, time, order, and result.

cards.front: What must a verbatim read-back include?
cards.back: Drug or intervention, dose, route, and any condition attached, such as 'only if the systolic stays above 100.'

cards.front: Can a physician order expand your scope of practice?
cards.back: No. Scope is set by the state, in New Jersey by the Office of Emergency Medical Services. An out-of-scope order is invalid no matter who gives it.

cards.front: How do you question an order you believe is unsafe?
cards.back: Lead with the observation: 'His systolic is 84 and he is diaphoretic. Do you still want the nitroglycerin?' That usually surfaces a detail the physician lacked.

cards.front: What do you document after taking a verbal order?
cards.back: The ordering physician's name, the exact order, the time it was given, the time it was carried out, and the patient's response.

cards.front: Name four common reasons to contact online medical direction.
cards.back: An intervention requiring authorization, a high-risk refusal, a resuscitation withhold or termination question, and a presentation that fits no protocol.

cards.front: What do you do with a vague order like 'give whatever he needs'?
cards.back: Clarify before acting. Ask for the specific drug, dose, route, and conditions, and read back the clarified order.

cards.front: What is a near miss and why report it?
cards.back: An error caught before reaching the patient. Reporting it gives the system the lesson without the injury, which is the cheapest learning available.

cards.front: What are the three categories in just culture and their responses?
cards.back: Human error: fix the system and console. At-risk behavior: coach and remove the incentive. Reckless behavior: discipline.

cards.front: What are the five steps after a medication error?
cards.back: Assess and treat the patient, tell the receiving clinician immediately, document facts in the chart, notify your supervisor, and file the incident report separately.

cards.front: Should the incident report be referenced in the patient's chart?
cards.back: No. The incident report is a separate quality process document. The chart records clinical facts: what was given, when, the response, and who was notified.

cards.front: What are the four parts of the DESC script?
cards.back: Describe the specific behavior, express the concern as an effect, suggest an alternative, and state the positive consequence. Done privately, soon, and once.

cards.front: When do you skip DESC and escalate immediately?
cards.back: When it is a patient safety issue in the moment. Use the two-challenge rule: state the concern twice, then escalate up the chain without delay.

cards.front: Why is concealing an error worse than the error itself?
cards.back: Audit trails and amendments are visible, honest error rarely ends a career under just culture, and concealment converts a system problem into misconduct.

cards.front: What reading level should patient communication target?
cards.back: About a 5th to 6th grade level: short sentences, one idea each, concrete nouns, most important point first and repeated at the end.

cards.front: Why are 'negative' and 'positive' risky words with patients?
cards.back: Patients commonly hear negative as bad news and positive as good news, which is the reverse of the clinical meaning. Say 'the test did not find it' instead.

cards.front: How should teach-back be phrased?
cards.back: Put the burden on yourself: 'I want to be sure I explained that well. Tell me what you will watch for tonight.' Never 'do you understand?'

cards.front: Name four signs a patient cannot read the form you handed them.
cards.back: Forgot my glasses, handing it to a relative, saying they will read it later, tracing without reading, signing without looking, or an incompletely filled form.

cards.front: How do you handle low literacy without embarrassing the patient?
cards.back: Make reading aloud your routine for everyone: 'I read these out loud for everybody, the print is small.' Then confirm with teach-back.

cards.front: A patient speaks some English. When do you still use an interpreter?
cards.back: For anything consequential: consent, refusal, risks, allergies, and history. Partial fluency collapses under stress and pain. Offer, do not ask if they need one.

cards.front: What do you say to an interpreter who is summarizing?
cards.back: 'Please give me everything she said, word for word.' Summarized interpretation drops the detail you are trying to collect.

quiz.q: A patient's son is shouting in the doorway that it took your crew too long to arrive while his mother sits pale and short of breath. What is the best first action?
choices: Explain the dispatch and traffic delays in detail
Let him speak briefly without defending, name the emotion, then give him a specific task
Ask him to step outside so you can work
Tell him the complaint process is available at headquarters
quiz.why: Listening and naming defuses faster than facts, and a task restores the control he lost. Explanations early and removal both escalate, and deferring to a complaint process ignores him.

quiz.q: Resuscitation has been stopped on a 66-year-old at home and the physician asks you to stay with the wife. She asks what happened. Which response is best?
choices: He passed away peacefully, he's in a better place now
We lost him, but at least it was quick
It was probably a massive heart attack and nothing could have been done
I have very difficult news. He died. I am so sorry.
quiz.why: A warning shot followed by plain words and silence is the standard. The others use softened language, offer false comfort, or speculate about a cause you cannot know.

quiz.q: A mother insists her 2-year-old 'is not acting right,' but the child looks well to you with normal vital signs. What is the correct approach?
choices: Treat the statement as a clinical finding, complete a careful assessment, and strongly recommend evaluation
Reassure her the child is fine and offer a refusal form
Document maternal anxiety and clear the call
Recheck vitals once and then leave if unchanged
quiz.why: Parental concern about a subtle change is a reliable pediatric red flag, and children compensate until they fail suddenly. The other options substitute your snapshot for her baseline knowledge.

quiz.q: A family member becomes upset that a previous crew 'did everything wrong' last week. What is the most professional response?
choices: Agree that the previous crew made mistakes
Defend the previous crew's actions in detail
State that you cannot speak to what happened before you arrived, then focus on what you are doing now
Advise them to file a lawsuit
quiz.why: Criticizing or defending another provider you did not observe is speculation that ends up in a record. Redirecting to current care is honest and keeps the call moving.

quiz.q: A 52-year-old who drank four beers fell down three stairs and struck his head. He is oriented, unsteady, takes warfarin, and says 'nothing's wrong, I just want to go to bed.' Which action is correct?
choices: Accept the refusal since he is oriented
Have him sign the refusal form and clear
Perform a breath alcohol test to determine capacity
Ask him to state in his own words what could happen if he stays home, and if he cannot, treat under implied consent and contact medical direction
quiz.why: Capacity is functional, not a number, and warfarin plus a head strike makes this a high-stakes refusal. A signature from someone who cannot state the risk is worthless.

quiz.q: An 86-year-old with moderate dementia says yes to transport, then no, then yes again over six minutes. What does this establish?
choices: She cannot communicate a consistent choice, so capacity is absent for this decision
She has capacity because she is verbal and alert
Her most recent answer is binding
Her first answer is binding
quiz.why: A consistent choice is one of the four capacity elements. Absent that, you seek the authorized decision maker or act under implied consent for an emergency.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old is injured at a friend's house. The friend's mother is present; the patient's parents cannot be reached. The teen has a deformed forearm and wants to go to the hospital. What is correct?
choices: Wait on scene until a parent is reached
Have the friend's mother sign consent as the adult present
Transport under implied consent, documenting the attempts to reach a guardian
Have the 16-year-old sign consent for himself
quiz.why: The friend's mother is not a legal guardian and a non-emancipated 16-year-old cannot consent. Implied consent covers the emergency while you document attempts to reach the guardian.

quiz.q: Which minor may legally consent for their own care in New Jersey?
choices: A 17-year-old who lives alone and works full time
A 16-year-old who is married
A 15-year-old whose parents are on vacation
A 17-year-old with a driver's license
quiz.why: Marriage is a recognized emancipation category, along with being pregnant or a parent, active military duty, or a court declaration. Living alone, working, or driving do not emancipate.

quiz.q: A father refuses transport for his 4-year-old who has a respiratory rate of 48, retractions, and a saturation of 89 percent. What is the correct action?
choices: Document the refusal and clear the scene
Have him sign a refusal and advise him to see the pediatrician tomorrow
Ask a neighbor to convince him
Contact online medical direction immediately, involve police if needed, and consider a report to the state child abuse hotline
quiz.why: A parent may not refuse care that endangers a child. This requires physician involvement, potentially law enforcement, and in New Jersey any person with reasonable cause must report suspected neglect.

quiz.q: Which narrative line would be strongest in a patient care report?
choices: Vitals were stable throughout transport
Patient tolerated the oxygen well
Vitals 1422: HR 96, BP 148/88, RR 20, SpO2 94 percent room air. Vitals 1435: HR 88, BP 138/84, RR 18, SpO2 97 percent on 2 L nasal cannula
Patient improved after treatment
quiz.why: Two timed sets with values prove the trend and the response to treatment. The other three are conclusions with no verifiable content.

quiz.q: Which documentation of a medication is complete?
choices: Aspirin 324 mg chewed at 1424, no adverse effect noted, pain unchanged at 8/10
Gave aspirin per protocol
Aspirin administered, patient tolerated well
Aspirin given on scene
quiz.why: Dose, route, time, and the documented response are all required. The others omit at least two of the four and record an opinion instead of an effect.

quiz.q: Why is 'care transferred to ED staff' a documentation problem?
choices: It is too informal for a legal record
It identifies no person or role, so nothing proves care was accepted by an equal or higher level of training
It omits the patient's insurance information
It should appear in the vital signs section
quiz.why: Abandonment turns on transfer to a named equal-or-higher provider. Without name, role, and time, the record cannot rebut the claim.

quiz.q: A narrative reads: 'Patient was uncooperative and rude throughout.' What is the best correction?
choices: Leave it; behavior is relevant
Change it to 'patient had a poor attitude'
Replace it with the patient's own quoted statements and the specific observed behaviors
Delete the sentence and note that the patient was difficult
quiz.why: Quotes and observed behaviors are evidence; character judgments are opinions that damage the chart and the patient's later care. Rewording the label does not fix it.

quiz.q: Which item should be omitted from a radio report to the receiving hospital?
choices: The trend between two sets of vital signs
The request for a trauma team on arrival
The treatment given and the patient's response
The patient's full name and home address
quiz.why: Identifiers add nothing to the receiving team's preparation and radio traffic is not private. The other three are exactly what the report exists to convey.

quiz.q: You are transporting a 24-year-old ejected from a vehicle. Which opening best fits the MIST format?
choices: Mechanism: unrestrained driver, frontal impact at highway speed, ejected, prolonged extrication
Patient is a 24-year-old male who lives on Third Street
The family says he has no medical history
We were dispatched at 2138 and arrived at 2146
quiz.why: MIST leads with mechanism because it predicts injuries the receiving team has not yet seen. Identifiers, negative history, and dispatch times do not shape their preparation.

quiz.q: Which detail is most important to include early in a cardiac arrest radio report?
choices: The patient's medication list
Whether the arrest was witnessed, bystander CPR, down time, and the initial rhythm
The name of the family member who called
The address of the residence
quiz.why: Witnessed status, bystander CPR, down time, and initial rhythm drive the receiving team's expectations and preparation more than any other information.

quiz.q: Which two elements are specific to a pediatric radio report?
choices: Blood pressure and temperature
Allergies and last oral intake
Weight in kilograms and the pediatric assessment triangle
Glasgow Coma Scale and pupil size
quiz.why: Weight drives every pediatric dose and equipment size, and the assessment triangle communicates severity instantly. The other items appear in adult reports too.

quiz.q: During transport your partner asks over the radio whether the hospital wants 'the usual for this frequent flyer.' What is wrong with this transmission?
choices: It conveys an opinion about the patient on a recorded channel and gives the receiving team no clinical information
Nothing, it is efficient
It should have included the patient's name for clarity
It is acceptable if the patient cannot hear it
quiz.why: Radio traffic is recorded and discoverable, and labels bias the receiving team against the patient. The report must carry clinical data, not characterizations.

quiz.q: Your former partner, who was on the call with you but has since gone off shift, texts asking what the patient's diagnosis turned out to be. What is the correct response?
choices: Share it, since he was part of the care team on that call
Share it without the patient's name
Share it only if he promises not to repeat it
Decline, because his involvement in the patient's care has ended
quiz.why: Treatment access ends when involvement ends. Removing the name does not help when he already knows exactly which patient is meant.

quiz.q: A police officer at a crash scene asks you whether the driver appeared intoxicated. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Tell him what you observed clinically, since police are exempt from HIPAA
Provide scene and safety information, decline to share clinical findings, and refer the request to your supervisor or the facility's process
Refuse to speak to the officer at all
Give him a copy of the patient care report
quiz.why: Law enforcement presence is not by itself a HIPAA exception. Clinical disclosures generally require authorization, a legal mandate, or a warrant or court order.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a permitted use of protected health information?
choices: Presenting a fully de-identified case in a training class
Telling a neighbor about an interesting call on your street
Looking up your own hospital chart while at work
Photographing a monitor to show a friend later
quiz.why: De-identified information is not protected health information and education is an operations purpose. The other three are disclosures or accesses with no permitted purpose.

quiz.q: You discuss a patient's case in the ambulance bay and a visiting family from another patient overhears. How is this classified?
choices: Permitted incidental disclosure with no issue
A breach only if they recognized the patient
A violation, because reasonable safeguards were not used
Permitted, because the conversation was for treatment purposes
quiz.why: Incidental disclosure is tolerated only when reasonable safeguards are in place. A public conversation at conversational volume is a failure of safeguards.

quiz.q: Which action carries the highest risk of ending an emergency department technician's employment in the first year?
choices: Asking a nurse to repeat an order
Accessing the chart of a relative or a well-known patient out of curiosity
Requesting an interpreter for a patient with partial English
Documenting that a blood pressure was unobtainable
quiz.why: Access without a treatment relationship is captured by audit logs and is a firing offense at most hospitals. The other three are correct professional behaviors.

quiz.q: A physician gives you an order by radio for a medication with a specific condition attached. What must happen before you administer it?
choices: Administer it, then confirm the details after
Write it on the chart and administer it
Have your partner listen to the next transmission
Repeat the drug, dose, route, and condition back verbatim and receive confirmation
quiz.why: Verbatim read-back with confirmation closes the loop and catches misheard doses. Acting first and confirming later is precisely how wrong-dose errors occur.

quiz.q: An online physician orders an EMT to perform a procedure that is clearly outside the New Jersey EMT scope of practice. What should the EMT do?
choices: Perform it and document that the physician authorized it
Perform it only if the patient consents
Decline, explain that it exceeds their scope, and document the exchange
Perform it if the patient is critical
quiz.why: Scope is defined by the state, and a physician cannot expand it by radio. Performing the skill is a certification violation regardless of the outcome or the patient's condition.

quiz.q: Which is an example of offline medical direction?
choices: The standing order in your protocol allowing aspirin for suspected cardiac chest pain
A radio call to the emergency physician for permission to assist with nitroglycerin
A phone consult about a high-risk refusal
A physician directing a resuscitation by video
quiz.why: Offline direction is the physician medical director's written authorization given in advance. The other three are live consults, which is online direction.

quiz.q: You believe an order you just received is unsafe given a finding the physician may not have heard. What is the best response?
choices: Carry out the order and document your disagreement
Restate the key finding and ask whether the physician still wants the order
Refuse without explanation and end the transmission
Ask your partner to call a different physician
quiz.why: Leading with the observation gives the physician the missing data without framing it as an accusation, which is usually all that is needed.

quiz.q: You draw up the wrong medication but catch it before giving it. What should happen?
choices: Nothing, because the patient was not affected
Mention it to your partner only
Note it in the patient's chart as an error
Report it as a near miss through the agency's incident reporting process
quiz.why: Near misses are reported so the system can fix the conditions that produced them. The patient's chart records clinical facts, not incident-report content, and silence teaches nothing.

quiz.q: Under a just culture model, which behavior warrants discipline rather than coaching or system repair?
choices: Working a shift while impaired, knowingly disregarding a serious risk
Misreading a similar-looking label under time pressure
Skipping a second identifier because the unit was short staffed
Forgetting to document a time on a busy call
quiz.why: Conscious disregard of a known serious risk is reckless behavior. The second is human error, and the third and fourth are at-risk behaviors that call for coaching and system fixes.

quiz.q: Your partner contradicts your treatment decision loudly in front of the patient and family. What is the best handling?
choices: Correct your partner immediately in front of everyone
Stop care and let your partner take over
Address any immediate safety concern, finish the call professionally, then raise the behavior privately using specific examples
Report it to the supervisor without ever speaking to your partner
quiz.why: Bedside arguments damage the patient's confidence and end up in complaints. Safety issues get escalated in the moment; everything else is handled privately, specifically, and soon.

quiz.q: You have explained a high-risk refusal to a patient. Which question best confirms understanding?
choices: Do you understand the risks?
Does that make sense?
Any questions before you sign?
I want to be sure I explained it well. Tell me what could happen if you stay home tonight.
quiz.why: Yes-or-no questions get polite agreement. Asking the patient to state the risk in their own words is both the capacity test and the documentation you need.

quiz.q: A Spanish-speaking patient with limited English is refusing transport. Her adult son offers to interpret and says she understands enough English anyway. What should you do?
choices: Proceed in English since she says she understands
Use a qualified interpreter for the entire refusal conversation and document the interpreter and language
Let the son interpret and document that he did
Have her sign the form and note the language barrier
quiz.why: Consent and refusal require full comprehension, partial fluency fails under stress, and family members edit and have interests. A refusal obtained any other way cannot be defended.

scenarios.title: The family in the room: cardiac arrest at home
scenarios.intro: At 0640 you are dispatched to a private residence for a 66-year-old male in cardiac arrest. His wife is performing CPR with dispatcher coaching. A daughter and a teenage grandson are in the house. You are the crew chief on a two-EMT ambulance with an ALS unit five minutes behind you.

steps.prompt:
You enter a small living room. The wife is on the floor doing compressions, crying, and saying "I'm not doing it right." The daughter is on the phone. The grandson is standing in the doorway.

How do you take over?

choices.text: "You did exactly the right thing and you kept him going. I'm taking over compressions now. I need you right here to tell me what happened."
choices.feedback: Correct. You validate her effort, transfer the task cleanly, and convert her into your historian without sending her away.

choices.text: "Okay, everybody out, we need the room."
choices.feedback: You lose your only witness and the family's chance to be present. Clearing the room reflexively is a habit worth unlearning.

choices.text: Take over compressions silently and begin working without addressing her.
choices.feedback: Efficient but costly. She is holding the down time, the history, and the medication list, and she will remember being ignored.

steps.prompt:
CPR is in progress, the AED is applied, and it advises a shock. The wife says he collapsed "maybe eight minutes" before she called, that he has a heart condition, and asks, "Is he going to be okay?"

What do you say?

choices.text: "He's going to be fine, we got here fast."
choices.feedback: You do not know that, and if he dies she will remember this sentence for the rest of her life. Never promise an outcome.

choices.text: "His heart has stopped. We are doing everything we can right now, and the paramedics are two minutes out. I'll tell you what is happening as we go."
choices.feedback: Correct. Honest, specific, no promise, and it sets the expectation that you will keep her informed.

choices.text: "I can't answer that right now."
choices.feedback: True but cold, and it closes a door you will need open. Pair honesty with what you are doing and what comes next.

choices.text: "It's very serious, but people come back from this all the time."
choices.feedback: This dresses up a low-probability event as routine. Out-of-hospital arrest survival is modest, and false framing sets up a worse fall.

steps.prompt:
The daughter asks whether the family can stay in the room while you work. Your partner glances at you.

What is the right call?

choices.text: Let them stay, position them where they can see without blocking, and assign one crew member or first responder to stay with them and explain what is happening
choices.feedback: Correct. Family presence during resuscitation is supported when a dedicated person supports them and the work is not obstructed.

choices.text: Remove everyone to another room for their own good
choices.feedback: This is the old default. Many families describe being removed as a lasting harm, and presence with support is generally the better option.

choices.text: Let them stay with no one assigned to them and continue working
choices.feedback: Presence without support is the worst of both. Unattended family in a resuscitation get in the way and get traumatized.

steps.prompt:
ALS arrives. After 28 minutes of resuscitation, asystole persists, end-tidal carbon dioxide has stayed at `8`, and the paramedic contacts online medical direction, who authorizes termination of efforts. The paramedic asks you to help tell the family.

How does that conversation start?

choices.text: Say nothing and let the paramedic handle it entirely while you pack equipment
choices.feedback: Acceptable in that the physician-directed conversation belongs to the clinician, but leaving immediately to pack up reads as abandonment of the family.

choices.text: Move to a private space, sit down, give a warning sentence, then say plainly that he died, and stop talking
choices.feedback: Correct. Private space, warning shot, plain words, silence. The silence is what lets them absorb it.

choices.text: Tell them in the living room that "we did everything we could but he didn't make it"
choices.feedback: Softened language gets misheard, and the hallway or the room where the body lies is the wrong place to open the conversation.

steps.prompt:
After several minutes the wife asks, "Did I do the CPR wrong? Is that why?" The grandson asks whether his grandfather was in pain.

How do you answer?

choices.text: "Your compressions were the only reason he had any chance at all. He was unconscious immediately and was not aware of anything."
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts and both are truthful. Bystander CPR genuinely improves the odds, and an arrest patient is unconscious within seconds.

choices.text: "It's hard to say. Maybe if the compressions had been deeper."
choices.feedback: Harmful. Speculation here creates lifelong guilt, and it is not even accurate; her CPR was the best thing that happened to him.

choices.text: "I really can't discuss that, you'll have to ask the doctor."
choices.feedback: You are declining to answer two questions you can honestly answer. Deflection here reads as confirmation of her fear.

steps.prompt: You are documenting the call. Which narrative entry is written correctly?

choices.text: "Worked a code, family was very upset, called it, transferred to PD."
choices.feedback: No times, no numbers, no physician name, and an editorial comment about the family. This chart proves nothing.

choices.text: "Arrived 0646. Bystander CPR in progress on arrival per wife, estimated collapse 0632. Compressions continued, AED applied 0648, one shock advised and delivered 0649. ALS arrival 0651. Resuscitation continued per protocol; end-tidal CO2 sustained at 8. Termination of resuscitation authorized by Dr. Patel, online medical direction, at 0719. Time of death 0719. Family present with a crew member assigned throughout. Scene turned over to Officer Ruiz, Badge 214, at 0736."
choices.feedback: Correct. Times, findings, the named authorizing physician, family presence documented, and a named scene transfer.

choices.text: "Unsuccessful resuscitation of a 66-year-old male. Family declined further questions. Death likely due to massive myocardial infarction."
choices.feedback: You have recorded a diagnosis you cannot make and a characterization of the family instead of the facts of the resuscitation.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: in a resuscitation with family present, the clinical work and the communication work run in parallel, and both are graded. The wife's compressions were also your history source, so validating and keeping her close was clinically useful, not just kind.
