Family presence works when one person is assigned to them; presence without support is the version that traumatizes. When the news came, the structure held: private space, warning sentence, the plain word died, then silence. The two questions afterward, about blame and about suffering, are the two questions families always ask, and both had honest, reassuring answers available. The chart then carried times, the named physician who authorized termination, and a named scene transfer, because that document is the only version of this morning that will exist in a year.

scenarios.title: Privacy calls in a busy department
scenarios.intro: You are working as an emergency department technician on a Saturday evening. The department is full, hallway beds are in use, and over the next hour you face a series of privacy and professional-conduct decisions, each of which has a correct answer and a tempting wrong one.

steps.prompt:
You are getting vitals on a hallway patient when a woman approaches and says, "That's my neighbor Rosa. Is she okay? I can call her family."

What do you do?

choices.text: Confirm only that the patient is being cared for and direct her to the front desk, without confirming or discussing anything about Rosa
choices.feedback: Correct. You cannot confirm presence or condition to an unverified person, and facility directory rules are handled at the desk, not in the hallway.

choices.text: Tell her Rosa is stable so she stops worrying
choices.feedback: Even 'stable' confirms she is here and discloses condition to someone with no verified relationship or authority.

choices.text: Ask Rosa loudly whether it is okay to talk to her neighbor
choices.feedback: Doing this in a hallway discloses the relationship and the situation to everyone within earshot. Ask quietly if you ask at all.

steps.prompt:
A nurse asks you to take a patient's belongings to the lost-and-found and hands you a paper chart to "drop at the desk." The desk is unattended and you are being paged.

What do you do?

choices.text: Leave the chart face-down on the desk and go
choices.feedback: Face-down is not secured. An unattended chart on an open counter is unsecured protected health information regardless of orientation.

choices.text: Place the chart in the secured location or hand it to a staff member, then answer the page
choices.feedback: Correct. Thirty seconds of delay is cheaper than an unsecured record, and handing it to a person closes the loop.

choices.text: Carry the chart with you to the next patient's room
choices.feedback: You have now taken one patient's record into another patient's room, which is a different exposure rather than a solution.

steps.prompt:
Your friend from high school is a patient in bed 14. You are not assigned to him. You are curious about why he is here, and the computer is open in front of you.

What do you do?

choices.text: Look at only the chief complaint, not the whole chart
choices.feedback: There is no partial-access exception. Every view is logged and the audit report does not distinguish curiosity from a quick peek.

choices.text: Do not access the record; if you want to know, greet him in person and let him tell you
choices.feedback: Correct. Access without a treatment relationship is a breach, and the audit log catches it. Asking the person is the only permitted route.

choices.text: Ask a nurse to tell you what is going on with him
choices.feedback: That is asking someone else to make the disclosure for you. The lack of a treatment relationship does not change because a colleague spoke it aloud.

steps.prompt:
You hand off a patient to the nurse: "Her pressure went from `124/78` at triage to `88/54` just now, and she's clammy." The nurse says, "She's fine, she's always like that, I'll get to her." Ten minutes pass and nobody has seen the patient.

What do you do?

choices.text: Repeat the concern once more, clearly and specifically, and if nothing happens escalate immediately to the charge nurse or the physician
choices.feedback: Correct. Two challenges then escalate, and a deteriorating patient does not wait for the chain of command to feel comfortable.

choices.text: Assume the nurse knows the patient better and wait
choices.feedback: Deference is not humility when the numbers are moving in the wrong direction. This is exactly the failure the two-challenge rule exists to prevent.

choices.text: Complain to a coworker about the nurse
choices.feedback: This addresses your frustration and not the patient. The patient still has a pressure of 88/54.

choices.text: Recheck the vitals and document them, then wait for the nurse
choices.feedback: Rechecking is good and documenting is required, but waiting after documenting a worse number is still a delay in care.

steps.prompt:
The patient is seen and moved to a resuscitation bay. Afterward the nurse says, in front of two coworkers, "You went over my head." 

How do you respond?

choices.text: "You told me she was fine and she wasn't. Maybe listen next time."
choices.feedback: Accurate and useless. Public correction guarantees the next concern you raise is received worse, not better.

choices.text: "Can we step over here for a second? Her systolic dropped 36 points in ten minutes and I got worried. I'd rather bring it to you first every time. How do you want me to flag something like that?"
choices.feedback: Correct. Private, specific, behavior-focused, and it ends with a request that builds the next handoff instead of winning this one.

choices.text: Apologize for escalating and say you will not do it again
choices.feedback: Do not apologize for escalating a deteriorating patient. You can be gracious about the how without disavowing the what.

steps.prompt:
At the end of the shift a coworker pulls out a phone and says, "Look at this X-ray from bed 14, you have to see it." The image has no name visible.

What do you do?

choices.text: Look, but do not let it be sent to you
choices.feedback: Viewing a photographed image of another patient's study is still access without a treatment relationship, and it endorses the behavior.

choices.text: Decline to look, say plainly that phone photos of patient images are a breach, and report it if it continues
choices.feedback: Correct. A photographed study on a personal phone is unsecured protected health information even with no name visible.

choices.text: Ask them to send it to you so you can study the finding later
choices.feedback: This creates a second unsecured copy on a second personal device, and now you own a breach too.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: every privacy decision in a department reduces to two questions. Does this person need this information to treat, bill for, or review this patient's care, and am I sharing only the minimum necessary? Neighbor, friend, unattended chart, and phone photo all fail the first question, and no amount of removing names rescues them. The second half of the case is a different skill with the same spine: state the observation, ask for what you need, and escalate on the second failure rather than the fifth. Escalating a deteriorating patient is never insubordination, and the way to keep the working relationship is to take the conversation off the floor afterward, make it specific, and end it with a request rather than a verdict.
